entries.lesson_core_move: Interpret |H(j\omega)| as the frequency-dependent amplitude scaling applied by a continuous-time LTI system to sinusoidal inputs, using its variation over \omega to identify which components are attenuated, passed, or amplified.

blocks.text: For a continuous-time LTI system, the magnitude response $|H(j\omega)|$ is the amplitude gain at frequency $\omega$. Read it as the factor that tells you how strongly the system scales a sinusoidal input at that frequency.

In the base case, start with one sinusoid $x(t)=A\cos(\omega_0 t)$ and read the gain at that same frequency. The output keeps the same frequency, and only the amplitude changes according to the magnitude response.

This gives the three basic interpretations of the curve: if $|H(j\omega)|<1$, that frequency is attenuated; if $|H(j\omega)|=1$, it is passed with the same amplitude; and if $|H(j\omega)|>1$, it is amplified.

So the first job in this topic is to read $|H(j\omega)|$ as a frequency-by-frequency amplitude scale. The next sections will use the same rule at one frequency, then two frequencies, and then across an entire magnitude-response curve.

example_content.example_prompt: An input $x(t)=6\cos(\omega_0 t)$ enters a system with $|H(j\omega_0)|=0.5$. Find the output amplitude.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a single sinusoid at frequency $\omega_0$ and a gain value given at that same frequency. For magnitude response, the output amplitude is the input amplitude multiplied by $|H(j\omega_0)|$.
So the output amplitude is $3$. The frequency stays $\omega_0$; only the amplitude changes when the system scales this sinusoidal input.

sections.section_title: Classifying One Frequency as Attenuated, Passed, or Amplified

example_content.example_prompt: At $\omega_0$, a system has $|H(j\omega_0)|=0.75$. Classify the component at that frequency as attenuated, passed, or amplified.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a single frequency $\omega_0$ with its gain value $|H(j\omega_0)|$ already given. To classify the component, compare that gain to 1 instead of computing a new output amplitude.
Here $|H(j\omega_0)|=0.75$, and $0.75<1$. That means the component at $\omega_0$ is attenuated.

sections.section_title: Comparing Magnitude Response at Two Frequencies

example_content.example_prompt: Given $|H(j\omega_1)|=0.4$ and $|H(j\omega_2)|=1.6$, compare the output amplitudes for the same sinusoidal input at $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is two gain values for the same sinusoidal input. Compare the gains directly, and keep the input amplitude the same at both frequencies so the output amplitudes differ only because of $|H(j\omega)|$.

Because $0.4<1$, the component at $\omega_1$ is attenuated. Because $1.6>1$, the component at $\omega_2$ is amplified. Since $1.6>0.4$, the output amplitude at $\omega_2$ is larger than the output amplitude at $\omega_1$ for the same input.

sections.section_title: Interpreting a Magnitude-Response Curve Across Frequency

image_slots.image_description: A clean instructional line plot of $|H(j\omega)|$ versus $\omega$ with a bold horizontal reference line at $|H(j\omega)|=1$. Draw one continuous magnitude-response curve that sits above 1 over a low-frequency band, stays near 1 over a middle band, and falls below 1 over a high-frequency band. Label the horizontal axis with $\omega$ and the vertical axis with $|H(j\omega)|$. Optionally mark one representative frequency in each band so the viewer can read the above, equal, and below-1 regions directly.

example_content.example_prompt: Using the magnitude-response plot, identify which frequency regions are attenuated, passed, and amplified by comparing the curve to the unity line.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a full magnitude-response curve, so read it by comparing each part of the curve to the unity line $|H(j\omega)|=1$. Do not classify the response from the slope or peak alone; the key test is whether the curve is above, on, or below 1.

Scan the curve region by region. Where the curve is above the unity line, the system amplifies those frequencies. Where it lies on the line, the system passes them. Where it falls below the line, the system attenuates them. Apply that same rule separately to the low-, middle-, and high-frequency bands.

For this plot, the low-frequency band is amplified, the middle band is passed, and the high-frequency band is attenuated. In plain language, the system boosts low frequencies, leaves a middle band roughly unchanged, and reduces high frequencies.

entries.lesson_core_move: Interpret \angle H(j\omega) as the frequency-dependent phase shift applied to each sinusoidal input component when using frequency response to characterize LTI filter behavior.

blocks.text: Phase response is the phase part of the frequency response. For a sinusoidal component at frequency $\omega_0$, $\angle H(j\omega_0)$ is the phase shift the system adds. It changes timing, not amplitude.

Use a single cosine input $x(t)=A\cos(\omega_0 t+\phi)$ so only one frequency and one phase adjustment are in play. The system keeps the same sinusoid frequency, scales the amplitude by $|H(j\omega_0)|$, and adds the system phase to the input phase.

With this sign convention, positive $\angle H(j\omega_0)$ advances the sinusoid and negative $\angle H(j\omega_0)$ delays it. Later examples will use that timing language directly when they read phase response.

sections.section_title: Reading \angle H(j\omega) at a Single Frequency

example_content.example_prompt: Given $H(j4)=3e^{j\pi/4}$, identify the phase shift experienced by a sinusoidal input at $\omega=4$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the single frequency $\omega=4$, and the response is already written in polar form as $H(j4)=3e^{j\pi/4}$. For phase response, read the angle, not the magnitude, because the angle is the phase shift at that frequency.
The argument of $H(j4)$ is $\pi/4$, so the phase shift at $\omega=4$ is $\pi/4$. In lead-or-lag language, this is a phase lead of $\pi/4$.

sections.section_title: Applying Phase Response to a Sinusoidal Component

example_content.example_prompt: If $x(t)=\cos(2t+\pi/4)$ and $\angle H(j2)=-\pi/6$, write the steady-state output phase for the sinusoidal component.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a single sinusoid at $\omega_0=2$: $x(t)=\cos(2t+\pi/4)$. Read the phase response at the same frequency, $\angle H(j2)=-\pi/6$, and keep the frequency fixed while you add the system phase to the input phase.
Add the phases: $\pi/4+(-\pi/6)=\pi/12$. So the steady-state output keeps the same frequency and uses the new phase $\pi/12$.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Positive and Negative Phase Shifts

example_content.example_prompt: If $\angle H(j3)=\pi/5$ and $\angle H(j8)=-\pi/5$, describe the phase change at each frequency in terms of lead or lag.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the sign of $\angle H(j\omega)$ at each frequency. A positive phase value means the output leads, or advances, the input. A negative phase value means the output lags, or delays, the input.
So at $\omega=3$, the output leads the input by $\pi/5$. At $\omega=8$, the output lags the input by $\pi/5$.

example_content.example_prompt: If $\angle H(j1)=\pi/6$ and $\angle H(j5)=-\pi/3$, determine which frequency component is more delayed and which is more advanced.

explanation_blocks.text: Read each phase shift first. At $\omega=1$, the phase is positive, so that component is advanced. At $\omega=5$, the phase is negative, so that component is delayed.

Now compare the sizes: $|\pi/6| < |\pi/3|$, so the delay at $\omega=5$ is larger in magnitude than the advance at $\omega=1$. The $\omega=5$ component is more delayed, and the $\omega=1$ component is more advanced.

entries.lesson_core_move: Evaluate low-frequency behavior by examining H(j\omega) as \omega approaches 0 and interpreting its magnitude and phase to decide how an LTI system scales, shifts, passes, or attenuates slowly varying inputs.

blocks.text: Low-frequency behavior means asking what the frequency response does near DC, so we examine $H(j\omega)$ as $\omega \to 0$. For slowly varying inputs, that neighborhood tells us the system's effective scaling and phase shift.
The value at $\omega = 0$, written $H(j0)$, is the DC reference point. Its magnitude gives the low-frequency gain, and its angle gives the low-frequency phase shift.

In the simplest base case, if $H(j\omega)=K$ near $\omega=0$, then a slow sinusoid $A\cos(\omega_0 t + \phi)$ comes out approximately multiplied by $|K|$ and shifted by $\angle K$. If $K$ is negative, that phase shift includes an inversion.
So the rule for the rest of the topic is fixed: read the limit at $\omega=0$, then interpret magnitude as scaling and phase as the shift applied to the slow part of the input.

sections.section_title: Evaluating the Low-Frequency Limit of H(j\omega)

example_content.example_prompt: Given $H(j\omega)=\frac{2-j\omega}{4+j\omega}$, evaluate $\lim_{\omega\to 0}H(j\omega)$ and state the low-frequency gain and phase.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the low-frequency limit, so we evaluate the transfer function at $\omega=0$. Because this rational expression is continuous there, direct substitution gives the DC value.
So $H(j0)=\frac{1}{2}$. The low-frequency gain is $\frac{1}{2}$, and the low-frequency phase is $0$ because the limit is a positive real number.
That means slowly varying input components are halved with no phase shift. For a slow sinusoid $A\cos(\omega_0 t + \phi)$, the output is approximately $\frac{1}{2}A\cos(\omega_0 t + \phi)$.

example_content.example_prompt: Suppose $H(j0)=\frac{1}{2}$. For a slowly varying sinusoidal input, decide whether the system attenuates, passes, or amplifies the component and by what factor.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the low-frequency gain, so we read the magnitude of $H(j0)$ directly. Here $|H(j0)|=\frac{1}{2}$, and the key comparison is with 1.
Since the magnitude is less than 1, the system attenuates the slowly varying sinusoidal component. The output amplitude is multiplied by $\frac{1}{2}$.
So the low-frequency magnitude scaling factor is $\frac{1}{2}$, and the classification is attenuation. In general, values below 1 attenuate, values equal to 1 pass, and values above 1 amplify.

example_content.example_prompt: Suppose $H(j0)=-2$. For a slowly varying sinusoidal input, determine the low-frequency phase shift and describe the resulting output component.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the low-frequency gain, and here the key feature is the negative sign in $H(j0)=-2$. A negative real constant has angle $\pi$, so the phase shift is an inversion rather than a delay.
The magnitude is 2, so the slow sinusoid is doubled in amplitude, and the phase adds $\pi$. That means the output keeps the same frequency but flips sign relative to the input.
So the low-frequency phase shift is $\pi$: the component is inverted while its amplitude is scaled by 2. The sign of $H(j0)$ gives the phase classification directly.

sections.section_title: Deciding How Slowly Varying Inputs Change Through the System

example_content.example_prompt: If $H(j0)=-\frac{3}{2}$ and $x(t)=A\cos(0.02t+\phi)$, describe the approximate output for this slowly varying component.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the low-frequency limit, so we read the slow sinusoid through the constant value $H(j0)=-\frac{3}{2}$. The magnitude gives the scaling and the negative sign gives a phase shift of $\pi$.
Apply both parts together: multiply the amplitude by $\frac{3}{2}$ and add $\pi$ to the sinusoid's phase. The output keeps the same slow frequency, but it is scaled up and inverted.
So the slowly varying input is amplified by $1.5$ and shifted by $\pi$. The combined low-frequency rule is to use the magnitude for scale and the sign for inversion.

entries.lesson_core_move: Evaluate high-frequency limits of |H(j\omega)| and \angle H(j\omega) to predict how an LTI system passes, attenuates, or phase-shifts rapidly varying sinusoidal components.

blocks.text: When $\omega$ is large, the question is not the full shape of $H(j\omega)$ but what $|H(j\omega)|$ and $\angle H(j\omega)$ approach. Those two limits are the high-frequency signature of the system, because they tell you whether a rapid sinusoidal component is passed, attenuated, or shifted.

For a sinusoidal component $A\cos(\omega_0 t+\phi)$, the output keeps the same frequency; only the amplitude and phase change. So once the high-frequency gain and phase are known, you can read the fate of the rapid component directly from $|H(j\omega)|$ and $\angle H(j\omega)$.

A simple first-order response such as $H(j\omega)=\frac{1}{1+j\omega}$ shows the base case: the dominant power of $j\omega$ controls the limit, the magnitude shrinks toward $0$, and the phase settles to a constant lag. That is the pattern you will reuse in the later high-frequency examples.

example_content.example_prompt: Evaluate $\lim_{\omega\to\infty}|H(j\omega)|$ for $H(j\omega)=\frac{3j\omega+2}{2j\omega-5}$ and decide whether very high-frequency components are attenuated, passed, or amplified.

explanation_blocks.text: This is a high-frequency magnitude question, so the cue is the limit as $\omega\to\infty$ of $|H(j\omega)|$. For a rational transfer function, the lower-order terms disappear at high frequency, so the leading powers of $j\omega$ determine the gain.

Now take the magnitude of the dominant coefficient ratio. Because the numerator and denominator have the same highest power of $j\omega$, the asymptotic magnitude is just the ratio of the leading coefficients.
Since $\frac{3}{2}>1$, the system amplifies very high-frequency sinusoidal components. This example stays on magnitude only; the phase limit is the next step.

example_content.example_prompt: Evaluate $\lim_{\omega\to\infty}\angle H(j\omega)$ for $H(j\omega)=\frac{1-j\omega}{1+j\omega}$ and interpret the asymptotic phase shift on a rapid sinusoid.

explanation_blocks.text: This is the phase version of the high-frequency test, so the cue is $\lim_{\omega\to\infty}\angle H(j\omega)$, not the magnitude. For a rational transfer function, the highest-power terms control the limiting angle because lower-order terms fade away.

Read the asymptotic angle of each leading factor: the numerator approaches $-\pi/2$ and the denominator approaches $\pi/2$. Subtracting the denominator phase from the numerator phase gives the constant high-frequency phase shift.
So the high-frequency phase limit is $-\pi$, which is a sign inversion of the rapid sinusoid. This example stays on phase only; the magnitude story was the previous step.

sections.section_title: Using Dominant Powers of j\omega in High-Frequency Limits

example_content.example_prompt: Use dominant powers of $j\omega$ to evaluate the high-frequency magnitude limit of $H(j\omega)=\frac{3(j\omega)^2-2j\omega+1}{(j\omega)^3+4(j\omega)^2-5}$.

explanation_blocks.text: This is a high-frequency magnitude question with extra lower-order clutter, so the cue is the degree mismatch in the rational transfer function. When $\omega$ is large, keep the highest powers of $j\omega$ and ignore the terms that vanish after factoring.
Cancel the common $(j\omega)^2$ factor. One power of $j\omega$ remains in the denominator, so the magnitude must decay toward zero no matter what the lower-order terms do.

So the high-frequency magnitude limit is $0$, which means the system attenuates rapidly varying sinusoidal components. The dominant-power shortcut is the point: the degree gap decides the limit before any full expansion is needed.

sections.section_title: Predicting Rapid-Sinusoid Output from High-Frequency Gain and Phase

example_content.example_prompt: For very large $\omega_0$, predict the output of $x(t)=3\cos(\omega_0 t-\pi/6)$ when the high-frequency limit of $H(j\omega)$ is $-2$.

explanation_blocks.text: This is the output-prediction version of the high-frequency test, so the cue is a rapid sinusoid together with the asymptotic gain and phase of $H(j\omega)$. At very large $\omega_0$, the output keeps the same frequency and only the amplitude and phase change.
Here $H(j\omega)\to -2$, so the high-frequency gain is $2$ and the phase shift is $\pi$. That means the rapid sinusoid is amplified by a factor of $2$ and shifted by a half cycle.

So the output is $6\cos(\omega_0 t+5\pi/6)$, which is the same-frequency sinusoid with doubled amplitude and a $\pi$ phase shift. This completes the transfer from asymptotic gain and phase to a concrete rapid-sinusoid output.

entries.lesson_core_move: Identify low-pass behavior in H(j\omega) by comparing its magnitude at low and high frequencies and interpreting strong low-frequency passage with high-frequency attenuation as the system preserving slow sinusoidal components while suppressing rapid ones.

blocks.text: A system has low-pass behavior when its magnitude response is larger at low frequencies than at high frequencies. The cue is the comparison of $|H(j\omega)|$ across frequency, not a phase pattern.

In the common base case, the low-frequency gain is close to $1$ while the high-frequency gain is much smaller. That means the same sinusoid is passed with little attenuation when it is slow and with much more attenuation when it is fast.

For a sinusoidal input at frequency $\omega$, the output amplitude is the input amplitude multiplied by $|H(j\omega)|$. So the system keeps slow sinusoidal components prominent and suppresses rapid ones.

That is the low-pass rule you will reuse: look at the magnitude response, compare low and high frequency gain, and classify the system by whether it preserves slow components more strongly than fast ones.

example_content.example_prompt: A system has $|H(j\omega_{\text{low}})| = 0.95$ at a small frequency and $|H(j\omega_{\text{high}})| = 0.08$ at a much larger frequency. What does that tell you about how the system treats slow and rapid sinusoidal components?

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the comparison of the two magnitudes, not the phase. Read the low-frequency value and the high-frequency value as gains for slow and rapid sinusoidal components.
Since $0.95$ is close to $1$ and $0.08$ is much smaller, the low-frequency component is passed with little attenuation while the high-frequency component is strongly reduced.
So the slow sinusoidal part stays prominent in the output, while the rapid sinusoidal part is suppressed. That is exactly the low-pass pattern.

example_content.example_prompt: At $\omega = 40$, the magnitude response is $|H(j40)| = 0.05$. What happens to a sinusoidal input at that frequency?

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the small magnitude at a high frequency. Read $|H(j40)| = 0.05$ as the gain applied to a rapid sinusoidal component.
That means the output keeps the same frequency $40$ but its amplitude is only $0.05$ of the input amplitude. The frequency stays the same; the size shrinks.
So the fast component is strongly attenuated. That is the high-frequency side of low-pass behavior.

example_content.example_prompt: A system has $|H(j\omega_{\text{low}})| = 1.1$ and $|H(j\omega_{\text{high}})| = 0.2$. Which frequency is passed more strongly, and what filter behavior does that imply?

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the comparison itself: read $|H(j\omega_{\text{low}})|$ and $|H(j\omega_{\text{high}})|$ side by side, then decide which one is larger.
Since $1.1 > 0.2$, the low-frequency component is passed more strongly. The larger low-frequency magnitude means the slow sinusoidal part survives much better than the fast one.
That contrast identifies low-pass behavior: the system preserves slow components and suppresses rapid components.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Low-Pass Behavior for Sinusoidal Components

example_content.example_prompt: An input is $x(t) = \cos(\omega_{\text{slow}} t) + \cos(\omega_{\text{fast}} t)$ with $\omega_{\text{slow}}$ small and $\omega_{\text{fast}}$ large. If $|H(j\omega_{\text{slow}})| \approx 1$ and $|H(j\omega_{\text{fast}})| \approx 0.1$, what does the output look like component by component?

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is to separate the input into its slow and fast sinusoidal parts, then attach the corresponding gain to each one.
Apply the low-pass rule to each component: the slow cosine keeps nearly full size, while the fast cosine is multiplied by a much smaller factor.
So the output is dominated by the slow variation, and the rapid variation is still present but strongly suppressed. That is the low-pass pattern in sinusoidal form.

entries.lesson_core_move: Classify high-pass behavior for an LTI filter from its magnitude response by comparing |H(j\omega)| at low and high frequencies and identifying low-frequency attenuation with high-frequency passage.

blocks.text: High-pass behavior means an LTI filter attenuates low-frequency components and preserves high-frequency components. In a magnitude response, that shows up as a small value of $|H(j\omega)|$ near $\omega=0$ and a larger value at higher $\omega$.

The test is a comparison between the low-frequency end and the high-frequency end of $|H(j\omega)|$. If the curve is lower near $\omega=0$ than it is farther to the right, the response is moving in the high-pass direction.
The clean prototype is a filter whose gain is near $0$ at low frequency and near $1$ at high frequency. That is the simplest model of high-pass behavior before the curve gets more complicated.

So the decision rule is simple: if the low-frequency gain is smaller than the high-frequency gain, classify the magnitude response as high-pass. Later sections will apply the same comparison to specific curves.

example_content.example_prompt: A filter has $|H(j\omega)| \approx 0.15$ for small $\omega$. What does that say about low-frequency components?

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the small value of $|H(j\omega)|$ near $\omega=0$. A gain of about $0.15$ is well below $1$, so the low-frequency end of the response is attenuating the signal.
That means a low-frequency component comes out with a much smaller amplitude than it went in. In other words, the system suppresses low-frequency content rather than passing it through unchanged.
This is the low-frequency side of a high-pass response: the low end is small, so the filter is already showing attenuation where $\omega$ is near zero.

example_content.example_prompt: A filter has $|H(j\omega)| \approx 0.95$ for large $\omega$. What does that say about high-frequency components?

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the large-$\omega$ end of the magnitude response. A value of $|H(j\omega)| \approx 0.95$ is close to $1$, so the high-frequency side is not being cut down very much.
That means a high-frequency component passes through with almost the same amplitude it had at the input. The response is showing high-frequency passage rather than strong suppression.

Do not call this amplification just because the component is passed. Passage means the amplitude is essentially preserved; amplification would require a gain above $1$. This is the high-frequency side of a high-pass response.

example_content.example_prompt: A filter has $|H(j\omega)| \approx 0.2$ near $\omega=0$ and $|H(j\omega)| \approx 1.1$ for large $\omega$. Compare the gains and state what the comparison means.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the pair of gains: $0.2$ near $\omega=0$ and $1.1$ for large $\omega$. Read them as the low-frequency gain and the high-frequency gain, then compare them directly.
The high-frequency gain is larger because $1.1 > 0.2$. The low-frequency side is well below $1$, so low frequencies are attenuated, while the high-frequency side is near $1$ and passes more strongly.
That means the magnitude response rises from low to high frequency, so the filter behaves like a high-pass filter.

sections.section_title: Classifying a Magnitude Response as High-Pass

example_content.example_prompt: A filter has $|H(j\omega)|$ small near $\omega=0$ and near $1$ for large $\omega$. Classify the filter from its magnitude response.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the pair of ends of the magnitude response: the low-frequency side is small and the high-frequency side is near $1$. Compare those two ends directly.
Because the low-frequency gain is much smaller than the high-frequency gain, low frequencies are attenuated while high frequencies pass. The response is not flat, so it is not all-pass.
That overall pattern is high-pass: the magnitude response suppresses low frequencies and preserves high frequencies, so the correct classification is high-pass rather than low-pass or band-pass.

entries.lesson_core_move: Classify a filter's passband behavior from its magnitude response by comparing low- and high-frequency gain to decide whether the LTI system is low-pass, high-pass, or neither.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Filter Interpretation from Magnitude Response

image_slots.image_description: A clean magnitude-response plot of $|H(j\omega)|$ versus $\omega$ with the low-frequency and high-frequency ends highlighted and a unity line at $|H(j\omega)|=1$. Horizontal axis labeled $\omega$, vertical axis labeled $|H(j\omega)|$, unity reference line at $|H(j\omega)|=1$, highlighted low-frequency end, highlighted high-frequency end, and a simple gain curve. Keep the graph uncluttered and instructional so the low-vs-high comparison is obvious at a glance.

blocks.text: A magnitude response shows how an LTI system scales sinusoidal inputs across frequency. For this step, read only the low-frequency end and the high-frequency end of $|H(j\omega)|$.
Use the unity line $|H(j\omega)|=1$ as the reference. Values above that line mean gain, and values below it mean attenuation.
If the low-frequency end is larger than the high-frequency end, the filter is low-pass. In that case, the system passes low frequencies more strongly than high frequencies.
If the high-frequency end is larger than the low-frequency end, the filter is high-pass. If neither end clearly dominates, the response is neither.
That is the rule you will reuse: read the two ends, compare them to each other and to the unity line, then classify the filter. The next sections will apply the same comparison to specific plots.

sections.section_title: Reading Low- and High-Frequency Gain from a Magnitude Response

image_slots.image_description: A magnitude-response plot with a visible low-frequency plateau around 1.5 and a high-frequency plateau around 0.4, plus a unity line at $|H(j\omega)|=1$. The horizontal axis is labeled $\omega$, the vertical axis is labeled $|H(j\omega)|$, and the curve is simple and uncluttered so the low-frequency end and high-frequency end are easy to compare at a glance.

example_content.example_prompt: From the displayed magnitude-response curve, read the low-frequency gain and the high-frequency gain and state which end is larger.

explanation_blocks.text: A magnitude-response plot shows how the system scales a sinusoid at each frequency. The cue in this step is the height of the curve at the low-frequency end and at the high-frequency end.

Read the left plateau as the low-frequency gain and the right plateau as the high-frequency gain. On this curve, the low-frequency end sits above the unity line, and the high-frequency end sits below it.

That means the low-frequency end is larger than the high-frequency end. The end-behavior comparison is the point of the example, because it gives you the same reading rule you will use again in the next step.

sections.section_title: Classifying a Low-Pass Filter from Magnitude Response

image_slots.image_description: A magnitude-response plot with horizontal axis labeled $\omega$ and vertical axis labeled $|H(j\omega)|$. The low-frequency end is clearly above the unity reference line at $|H(j\omega)|=1$, the high-frequency end is clearly below it, and the curve makes a smooth downward transition between the ends. Keep the plot uncluttered and omit any phase information or extra panels.

example_content.example_prompt: For the displayed magnitude-response curve, decide whether the filter is low-pass, high-pass, or neither.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the comparison between the low-frequency end and the high-frequency end of the magnitude-response curve. Start by reading the two ends, then use their ordering to classify the filter.
Here the low-frequency end sits above the unity line, while the high-frequency end sits below it. So the low-frequency gain is larger than the high-frequency gain.
By the rule from the previous step, that end comparison means the filter is low-pass. It passes low frequencies better than high frequencies.

sections.section_title: Classifying a High-Pass Filter from Magnitude Response

image_slots.image_description: A magnitude-response plot with horizontal axis labeled $\omega$ and vertical axis labeled $|H(j\omega)|$. The low-frequency end is clearly below the unity reference line at $|H(j\omega)|=1$, the high-frequency end is clearly above it, and the curve makes a smooth upward transition between the ends. Keep the plot uncluttered and omit any phase information or extra panels.

example_content.example_prompt: For the displayed magnitude-response curve, decide whether the filter is low-pass, high-pass, or neither.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is still the ordering of the two ends of the magnitude-response curve. Compare the low-frequency end and the high-frequency end, then classify the filter from that comparison.
Here the low-frequency end sits below the unity line, while the high-frequency end sits above it. So the high-frequency gain is larger than the low-frequency gain.
By the rule from the previous step, that end comparison means the filter is high-pass. It passes high frequencies better than low frequencies.

sections.section_title: Classifying Neither Low-Pass Nor High-Pass Behavior

image_slots.image_description: A magnitude-response plot with horizontal axis labeled $\omega$ and vertical axis labeled $|H(j\omega)|$. The low-frequency end and high-frequency end are at about the same sub-unity gain, both clearly below the unity reference line at $|H(j\omega)|=1$. The middle region rises into a clear hump above 1, so the response is not low-pass or high-pass. Keep the plot uncluttered and omit any phase information or extra panels.

example_content.example_prompt: For the displayed magnitude-response curve, decide whether the filter is low-pass, high-pass, or neither.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is still the comparison between the low-frequency end and the high-frequency end. Read those two ends first, because that is what determines low-pass and high-pass behavior.
Here the low-frequency end and the high-frequency end sit at about the same height, and both are below the unity line. The middle hump does not change that end comparison.
Since neither end is larger, the curve does not match the low-pass pattern and it does not match the high-pass pattern either. The correct classification is neither low-pass nor high-pass.
